description:
Companion that turns your phone into a wireless Wi-Fi gamepad for your PC.


V-Pad Helper — the companion app for V-Pad on iPhone. Windows and macOS.
What this release fixes
Connecting by QR now works on PCs with virtual network adapters. If you run VirtualBox, VMware, WSL, Hyper-V, Docker or a VPN, the QR code could carry an address your phone had no way of reaching, and the connection would simply time out — connecting sometimes, failing most of the time. The helper now recognises those adapters and puts your real LAN address in the code.
The phone reconnects by itself after the helper restarts. The pairing used to be remembered by address and port, and the port changes every time the helper starts, so the phone could never find the computer again on its own and you had to re-scan the code — often daily. The code now carries the computer's network name, which survives both a restart and a new address from your router.
The second fix needs V-Pad 2.0.7 or newer on the phone to take effect. Everything else works with any version, and an older phone pairs with this helper exactly as before.

Windows
1. Download V-Pad-Helper-Setup.exe and run it.
   It installs for your user only, so it does not ask for administrator rights, and it puts an uninstaller in Add/Remove Programs. The app itself lives in the system tray.
2. If the tray offers "Install gamepad driver", accept it once (ViGEmBus — this is what lets games see a real Xbox controller). That step does need administrator rights, because it installs a driver.
3. On the iPhone: open V-Pad → Connection → tap this computer.
Keep the phone and the PC on the same Wi-Fi network. Windows will ask once whether the app may use the network — allow it on private networks, otherwise the phone can see the computer but not connect. If the phone can see the computer but still cannot connect, open the tray menu and choose Allow through Windows Firewall… (one prompt).

macOS
V-Pad-Helper.dmg is current again — the first macOS build since v0.2.1 in August. The old one ran a helper from before pairing existed, so no recent version of the V-Pad app could connect to it at all.
Open the DMG and drag V-Pad Helper to Applications before running it. That step matters here: the app asks for Accessibility permission to move the mouse and press keys, and macOS ties that permission to where the app lives — grant it while the app is still in your Downloads folder and the permission will not follow the copy you move later.
The app is signed and notarized by Apple, so it opens without a Gatekeeper warning.
On a Mac the pad drives the keyboard and mouse rather than a virtual Xbox controller: left stick to WASD, D-pad to the arrows, right stick to the mouse, triggers to clicks. Apple grants no third-party app a virtual gamepad, so a game that insists on a real controller will not find one on a Mac. Windows does have the real thing.
